title: Trachea Pulled Towards a Dull Base / Collapse Needs a Cause: Think Bronchial Carcinoma First

blocks.text: Trachea Pulled Towards a Dull Base / Collapse Needs a Cause: Think Bronchial Carcinoma First

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-14 · Physical examination · PACES Station 1, respiratory examination encounter · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 min: up to 6 min examining, then at least 4 min of examiner questions · Guidelines: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (published 23 June 2015; last updated 15 April 2026) · Related AMaC: Respiratory examination: pleural effusion; pneumonectomy

A 67-year-old man, a retired lorry driver, attends with a cough for three months and breathlessness. He smoked for 40 years. Please examine his respiratory system and report what you find. You have up to 6 minutes to examine, followed by questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A trachea pulled towards the side with reduced expansion and a dull base suggests collapse of the lung on that side, probably the right lower lobe on these findings; the lesson is to tell it from an effusion and to say a bronchial tumour must be excluded, without telling him cancer is established.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates call any dull base an effusion, or forget the trachea. Pass: find the trachea pulled towards the dull side, say collapse, and name cancer as the cause to exclude. Fail: effusion, or no cause given.

Where is the trachea, and what does the chest do?
"I'm going to feel your windpipe and your chest, then tap and listen."
Trachea; expansion; percussion; tactile or vocal resonance; breath sounds; back.

Supraclavicular nodes, Horner's, hoarse voice, SVC signs, liver.
Say what it is and the plan.
"These findings suggest right-sided volume loss or collapse; the likely cause is a blockage, so I'd arrange urgent imaging."

Trachea pulled to the right; reduced right basal expansion; dull right base; reduced breath sounds; no wheeze
Adds quiet breath sounds with reduced vocal resonance over the collapsed lobe (blocked bronchus), no effusion signs, no clubbing and no Horner's

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing.
Not used for this station type: the patient is a real or simulated patient and the findings are in section 8.

Findings (released as each step is done). Tar-stained fingers; no clubbing. Respiratory rate 18; saturation 94% on air (scenario values). Trachea deviated to the right. Reduced expansion over the right base. Percussion dull at the right base. Breath sounds quiet at the right base and vocal resonance reduced there (the bronchus is blocked). No wheeze. No supraclavicular nodes. No Horner's syndrome.

Question ladder. Q1 Findings and diagnosis (R3, R4): probable right lower lobe collapse; examination alone cannot prove the lobe, so imaging defines the site. Q2 Distinction (R4): effusion pushes the trachea away and is stony dull; collapse pulls it towards. Q3 Causes (R5): bronchial carcinoma, mucus plug, foreign body, nodal compression. Q4 Investigation (R6): chest X-ray, CT chest and bronchoscopy; NICE NG12 advises an urgent direct-access chest X-ray for people aged 40 and over who have ever smoked and have unexplained cough or breathlessness (1.1.2), and a suspected cancer pathway referral when the X-ray suggests lung cancer (1.1.1). Q5 Advice (R7): stop smoking; report haemoptysis.
Normal-findings variant. Central trachea and symmetrical chest. The candidate must say the respiratory examination is normal.
Curveball 1. "The trachea is pushed away and the base is stony dull." (R4) Safe: that is a pleural effusion, not collapse.
Curveball 2. "He coughs up blood." (R5) Safe: haemoptysis needs urgent referral for suspected lung cancer.
Curveball 3. "He has noisy breathing (stridor) at rest." (R5) Safe: possible central airway obstruction; emergency senior and airway assessment the same day.

Fail performance
(Lays him flat; percusses the front only. [R1 Fail] Does not feel the trachea. [R2 Fail])
CANDIDATE: The trachea is pushed away with a stony dull base. [R3 Fail] It's an effusion. [R4 Fail] I can't say why. [R5 Fail]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: Wait and see. [R6 Fail] No advice. [R7 Fail]
Examiner note: Wrong trachea, wrong diagnosis and no tests.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your chest? I'll sit you up and we'll pause if you get breathless. [R1 Pass]
(Feels the trachea; compares expansion; percusses and listens front and back. [R2 Pass])
CANDIDATE: The trachea is pulled to the right, with reduced right basal expansion, a dull right base and reduced breath sounds. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]

CANDIDATE: This is probably right lower lobe collapse; imaging will confirm the site. [R4 Pass] Bronchial carcinoma is the cause to exclude first, but a mucus plug or an inhaled foreign body are others. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: A chest X-ray, CT chest and bronchoscopy. [R6 Pass]
EXAMINER: And advice?
CANDIDATE: I can't say what this is yet; the scans and bronchoscopy will tell us. Stop smoking, and tell us at once about coughing up blood or worsening breathlessness. [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and accurate. Did not cite NICE or explain the effusion distinction.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? I'll explain each step. [R1 High]
(Feels the trachea from the front gently; examines the back systematically; checks nodes. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: Quiet breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance over the dull base, no clubbing, no Horner's, no effusion signs. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Probable right lower lobe collapse, not an effusion, because the trachea is pulled, not pushed. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Carcinoma first, given 40 years of smoking; nodal compression and post-obstructive infection are alternatives. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: An urgent chest X-ray, CT, bronchoscopy, and discussion at the lung cancer multidisciplinary team; NICE NG12 supports referral if the film suggests cancer. [R6 High]
EXAMINER: And advice?
CANDIDATE: Offer smoking-cessation support, check he is fit for bronchoscopy, and explain what each result means. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: Thank you for letting me examine you. [R1 High]
Examiner note: Distinguished collapse from effusion and named the cause.
R4: Calling collapse an effusion ignores the pulled trachea.
R5: Giving no cause misses cancer in a heavy smoker.
R2: Not feeling the trachea loses the key sign.
R6: Waiting to see if it clears delays a possible cancer diagnosis.
R3: Reporting a pushed trachea shows signs were assumed.
"Let me feel where the trachea is."
"The trachea is pulled towards the dull side."
"I'd arrange urgent imaging."

Lobar collapse: trachea pulled towards the affected side, reduced expansion, dull percussion, and quiet breath sounds with reduced vocal resonance when the bronchus is blocked (bronchial breathing if it is patent). Examination cannot prove which lobe has collapsed; chest X-ray and CT define the site and cause. In an older smoker, investigate an obstructing cancer urgently without saying cancer is established. Effusion: trachea central or pushed away, stony dull, absent breath sounds.

NICE NG12 (published 23 June 2015; last updated 15 April 2026): offer an urgent direct-access chest X-ray to people aged 40 and over who have ever smoked and have one or more unexplained symptoms such as cough or breathlessness (1.1.2); consider one for chest signs consistent with lung cancer (1.1.3); use a suspected cancer pathway referral for chest X-ray findings that suggest lung cancer, or for unexplained haemoptysis aged 40 and over (1.1.1).
THINK: Trachea pulled; collapse; cancer.
SAY: "Probable right lower lobe collapse; bronchial carcinoma first."
DO: Trachea; expansion; percuss; listen; back; nodes.
NUMBERS: Saturation 94% on air (scenario).
TRAP: Calling it an effusion.
FINISH: X-ray; CT; bronchoscopy; stop smoking.
